Secondary thermophilic microaerobic treatment in the anaerobic
digestion of corn straw
Shan-Fei Fu a,b, Xiao-Shuang Shi a, Xiao-Hui Xu a, Chuan-Shui Wang a, Lin Wang a, Meng Dai a,
Rong-Bo Guo a,⇑
a Shandong Industrial Engineering Laboratory of Biogas Production & Utilization, Qingdao Institute of Bioenergy and Bioprocess Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences,
Qingdao, Shandong Province 266101, PR China
b University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100049, PR China
h i g h l i g h t s
 Secondary thermophilic microaerobic treatment (STMT) was carried out.
 STMT obviously improved the efﬁciency of the late fermentation stage.
 Corn straw with STMT obtained 28.45% higher methane yield.
 The VS removal efﬁciency after STMT improved for 29.43%.

a b s t r a c t
Thermophilic microaerobic pretreatment (TMP) has been proved to be an alternative pretreatment
method during anaerobic digestion (AD) of corn straw. In this study, in order to improve the fermentation
efﬁciency during late AD stage, improve the methane yield and volatile solid (VS) removal efﬁciency, a
secondary thermophilic microaerobic treatment (STMT) was applied in the late AD stage of corn straw.
Results showed STMT obviously improved the fermentation efﬁciency, methane yield and VS removal
efﬁciency. The maximum methane yield and maximum VS removal efﬁciency were simultaneously
obtained when the oxygen loads during STMT was 10 ml/g VS (VS of residual substrate). The maximum
methane yield was 380.6 ml/g VSsubstrate, which was 28.45% and 10.61% higher than those of untreated
and once thermophilic microaerobic pretreated samples, respectively. The maximum VS removal efﬁ-
ciency was 81.85%, which was 29.43% and 17.23% higher than those of untreated and once thermophilic
microaerobic pretreated samples, respectively.

1. Introduction
Due to the increasing attentions to renewable energy, climate
change and waste management, anaerobic digestion (AD) as an
ideal way for the comprehensive utilization of organic waste has
been widely employed (Sanscartier et al., 2012). Corn straw, which
is rich in cellulose, hemicelluloses and lignin, is one of the largest
residues from agriculture. It has a great potential for biogas pro-
duction because of its abundance and high carbohydrate content
(You et al., 2014). However, the strong interlinkage of cellulose,
hemicelluloses and lignin with noncovalent forces and covalent
cross-linkage gives a stable shape and structure to the plant
(NIZAMI et al., 2009), which are the barriers of the enzymolysis
during hydrolysis process. Therefore, the AD of corn straw is inefﬁ-
cient. Pretreatment is essential to decrease the structural and
compositional barriers by breaking down lignin interference,
reducing cellulose crystallinity and increasing surface area (Yu
et al., 2014).
Recently, microaerobic pretreatment has been proved to be an
efﬁcient pretreatment method for the anaerobic digestion in sev-
eral studies (Botheju et al., 2010; Charles et al., 2009; Fu et al.,
2015; Mshandete et al., 2005). The term microaeration refers to
the controlled introduction of small amounts of oxygen into an
anaerobic biochemical process to enable both anaerobic and aero-
bic biological activities to occur within a single bioreactor (Lim
et al., 2014). Compared to other methods, microaerobic pretreat-
ment is more economy and environmental friendly, which just

needs limited amount of oxygen (or air) supplied directly into the

In our earlier paper study on the effect of thermophilic
microaerobic pretreatment on the anaerobic digestion of corn
straw, the thermophilic microaerobic pretreatment before anaero-
bic digestion of corn straw at the oxygen loads of 5 ml/g VSsubstrate
demonstrated a 16.24% higher methane yield (Fu et al., 2015).
However, the VS removal efﬁciency at this condition was only
68.06%, which means there are still a relevant portion of corn straw
that were not been digested. During anaerobic digestion of cellulo-
sic substrate like corn straw, easily degradable compounds are
ﬁrstly utilized at the early stage of AD, the residual recalcitrant
compositions are mainly utilized at the late stage of fermentation,
and thus the fermentation at the late stage is inefﬁcient. In order to
improve the fermentation efﬁciency during the late stage, a sec-
ondary thermophilic microaerobic treatment (STMT) was proposed
in this study. The secondary thermophilic microaerobic treatment
at the later period of anaerobic digestion when obvious decreases
in daily methane yield were appeared could be a solution to
improve the low fermentation efﬁciency during the late stage.
The objective of this study was to investigate the effect of the
secondary thermophilic microaerobic treatment on the anaerobic
digestion of corn straw. In addition, different oxygen loads during
secondary thermophilic microaerobic treatment were also applied
to investigate the effect of oxygen load on the performance of sec-
ondary thermophilic microaerobic treatment.
2. Methods
2.1. Substrate and inoculum
The substrate used in this study was corn straw, which was col-
lected from corn ﬁeld in Pingdu (Shandong Province, China). The
corn straw was chopped and sieved to a size of less than 0.5 cm
by a 0.5 cm sieve. The total solid (TS) and volatile solid (VS) of corn
straw were 92.44% and 93.44% (based on TS), respectively. The C/N
and C/H ratio are 28.97 and 7.73, respectively (The Element con-
tents of corn straw were quantiﬁed with an elemental analyzer,
Vario EL Cube). The proportions of cellulose, hemicelluloses and
lignin are 45.43%, 22.73% and 10.79% (% of TS), respectively.
Inoculum used in this study was biogas slurry, which was col-
lected from a 500 m3 size of biogas plant (Qingdao, Shandong
Province, China). The TS and VS contents of the biogas slurry are
6.10% and 73.05% (% of TS), respectively.
2.2. Thermophilic microaerobic pretreatment (TMP) of corn straw
The TMP stage total contained 10 bottles, the bottles were
divided into 5 groups (marked as R0, R, RS1, RS2 and RS3). R0
was used for testing the VS removal efﬁciency before STMT, R
was used for testing the biogas production from once thermophilic
microaerobic pretreated corn straw, RS1, RS2 and RS3 were used
for testing the effect of STMT on the anaerobic digestion of corn
straw. During TMP stage, 5.77 g corn straw and 22 ml inocula were
mixed in bottles, and then deionized water was added to reach a
total volume of 0.1 L. Each bottle was ﬂushed with N2 for 5 min
to replace the air, and then the bottles were closed with rubber
stoppers. Then 25 ml oxygen at atmospheric pressure was injected
to the bottles with a syringe to reach the oxygen loads of 5 ml/g VS
substrate, which was regarded as the optimized oxygen loads in
previous study (Fu et al., 2015). The bottles were placed in a shak-
ing water bath at 55 C with 130 rpm. The oxygen levels were mea-
sured by a gas chromatograph (SP 6890, Shandong Lunan Inc.,
China) every 4 h until the oxygen was consumed completely.
2.3. Batch anaerobic digestion tests
Batch mesophilic (37 C) anaerobic digestion tests was per-
formed in duplicates, the bottles after thermophilic microaerobic
pretreatment were added with another 22 ml inocula to reach a
relation TSinoculum/TSsubstrate of 0.5, and deionized water was added
to reach a total volume of 0.2 L. Another 2 bottles (marked as A)
were also employed to ﬁnd out the biogas yield from corn straw
without pretreatment. The bottles were placed in a shaking water
bath at 37 C with 130 rpm.
2.4. Secondary thermophilic microaerobic treatment (STMT)
STMT of fermentation system was carried out when obvious
decrease in daily methane yield was appeared. The VS removal efﬁ-
ciency before STMT was tested according to R0. During STMT, oxy-
gen at atmospheric pressure was injected to RS1, RS2 and RS3 with
a syringe to reach the oxygen loads of 5, 10 and 20 ml/g VS (VS of
residual substrate). Then, the bottles were placed in a shaking
water bath at 55 C with 130 rpm for secondary thermophilic
microaerobic treatment. After STMT, another 22 ml inocula were
added into the bottles and ﬂushed with N2 for 5 min to replace
the air, and then the bottles were closed with rubber stoppers. At
last, the bottles were placed in shaking water bath at 37 C with
130 rpm to continue fermentation.
2.5. Analytical methods
The biogas yield was measured by water displacement method.
Biogas composition was measured by a gas chromatograph (SP
6890, Shandong Lunan Inc., China), equipped with a Porapak Q
stainless steel column (180 cm long, 3 mm outer diameter) and a
thermal conductivity detector. The temperatures of the injector,
detector and oven were 50, 100 and 100 C, respectively. The car-
rier gas was argon. SCOD (Soluble Chemical Oxygen Demand)
was measured after centrifuging at 10,000 rpm for 5 min and ﬁlter-
ing samples through a 0.45 lm glass microﬁber ﬁlter and deter-
mined by spectrophotometric method (SEPA, 2002). The element
contents of corn straw were detected with an elemental analyzer
(Vario EL Cube). TS, VS were determined according to standard
methods (APHA, 2006). Cellulose, hemicelluloses and lignin were
determined according to the method as Goering and van Soest
(1970) described.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Biogas and methane productions
The biogas and methane yields during anaerobic digestion of
corn straw were shown in Fig. 1. Daily methane yield increased
sharply at the initial stage of anaerobic digestion and reached the
maximum at the 9th day of AD. The maximum daily methane yield
of thermophilic microaerobic pretreated corn straw was about
57.0% higher than that of untreated sample. The methane produc-
tion peaks of thermophilic microaerobic pretreated corn straw
were between 4th and 18th day of AD. Comparatively, the methane
production peak of untreated corn straw was between 9th and
17th day of AD, which was lower and shorter. These means the
methane yield of thermophilic microaerobic pretreated corn straw
was quick and concentrated. In other words, the AD of ther-
mophilic microaerobic pretreated corn straw was more efﬁcient.
STMT was carried out at the 22th day of AD, when the daily
methane yield in thermophilic microaerobic pretreated corn straw
was obviously decreased. The VS removal efﬁciency at that time
was determined by R0, which was 41.3%. Then 15, 30, 60 ml

oxygen at atmospheric pressure was respectively added to RS1,
RS2, RS3 with a syringe to reach the oxygen loads of 5, 10, 20 ml/
g VS (VS of residual substrate) during secondary thermophilic
microaerobic treatment. The cumulative methane yields were
shown in Fig. 1C. The maximum cumulative methane yield was
380.6 ml/g VSsubstrate, which was obtained from RS2 and followed
by RS1, RS3, R and A. The methane yield of RS2 was 28.45% higher
than that of untreated sample, the methane yield of R was 16.14%
higher than that of untreated sample which was quite accordance
with the result reported in previous study (Fu et al., 2015). The
results in this study were quite different with that reported by
Mshandete et al. (2005). In their study, a second aerobic pulse in
the AD of sisal pulp gave a lower methane yield (94%) than the
one with only once aerobic pretreatment. In this study, secondary
thermophilic
microaerobic
treatment
gave
a
10.61%
higher
methane yield than that with only once thermophilic microaerobic
pretreatment. The reason for reduction of methane yield in the
study of Mshandete et al. (2005) may be the activity of methano-
gens was destroyed during secondary aeration treatment and there
was no reinoculation after secondary aeration treatment. In addi-
tion, because the amount of oxygen during secondary aeration
treatment was not accurately controlled, the excess organic sub-
strate consumed may be another reason for the decrease in
methane yield.
The cumulative methane yields before and after secondary ther-
mophilic microaerobic treatment were shown in Fig. 1D. The
cumulative methane yield of thermophilic microaerobic pretreated
corn straw before STMT was about 283.0 ml/g VSsubstrate, which
was 32.68% higher than that of untreated sample. As for the
cumulative methane yield after STMT, the maximum methane
yield was obtained when the oxygen loads during STMT was
10 ml/g VS (VS of residual substrate), which was 93.3 ml/g
VSsubstrate and 12.88% higher than that of untreated sample. In
addition, the cumulative methane yields of untreated sample and
RS2 after STMT were respectively 34.74% and 51.46% higher than
that of once thermophilic microaerobic pretreated sample, which
was only 61.6 ml/g VSsubstrate.
The cumulative methane yields of RS1 and RS3 after STMT were
also higher than that of once thermophilic microaerobic pretreated
sample, which meant the STMT process was surely improved the
methane yield of corn straw during the late stage of anaerobic
digestion. However, the increase in oxygen load during STMT did
not lead to high methane yield, which demonstrated once again
the importance of oxygen loads during microaerobic treatment.
On the one hand, the excessive oxygen may inhibit the activity of
methanogens and decrease the methane yield (Xu et al., 2014). In
addition, facultative organisms have higher growth rates and
would out-compete strict anaerobes under high oxygen levels
due to substrate competition (Lim and Wang, 2013). On the other
hand, insufﬁcient oxygen will not be strong enough to support the
growth of facultative organisms.
3.2. SCOD variations during anaerobic digestion
Soluble COD is a parameter that represents the extent of sol-
ubilization. Pretreatment methods that disintegrate the substrate
before digestion to improve the biogas yield during the subsequent
digestion are most commonly characterized in terms of solubiliza-
tion of COD (Appels et al., 2011). The variation of SCOD during
anaerobic digestion of corn straw was shown in Fig. 2. The average
SCOD of thermophilic microaerobic pretreated corn straw at the
ﬁrst day of anaerobic digestion was 7962.5 mg/L, which was
26.39% higher than that of untreated sample. The SCOD concentra-
tions of thermophilic microaerobic pretreated corn straw increased
sharply and reached the peak ﬁrstly. Comparatively, the SCOD con-
centrations peak of untreated sample came later. The earlier SCOD
concentrations peak in thermophilic microaerobic pretreated corn
straw means the fermentation structural and compositional bar-
riers of corn straw were disrupted partly during TMP.
The
SCOD
concentration
after
secondary
thermophilic
microaerobic treatment obviously increased, which could attribute
to the high hydrolysis under microaerobic condition. According to
Fig. 1A, the higher SCOD concentration in RS1, RS2 and RS3 also
resulted to the increase in daily methane yield. Increased SCOD
concentration under microaerobic condition was also reported by
Mshandete et al. (2005) and Jagadabhi et al. (2010), the reason
behind this may be the higher hydrolysis rate under microaerobic
condition.

3.3. VS removal efﬁciency
During the digestion process, VS are degraded to a certain
extent and converted into biogas and the degree of stabilization
is often expressed as the percent reduction in VS (Appels et al.,
2008). In this study, the VS removal efﬁciency was calculated as
following:
VS removal efficiency ¼ initial VS  remaining VS
initial VS
ð1Þ
where initial VS is the VS of substrate added, remaining VS is calcu-
lated by the remaining total VS in the fermentation bottles minus
the VS of blank (only inoculum).
The VS removal efﬁciencies of A, R, RS1, RS2 and RS3 were
63.24 ± 0.15%,
69.82 ± 1.94%,
81.09 ± 0.90%,
81.85 ± 0.94%
and
79.54 ± 0.94%, respectively. The VS removal efﬁciency of once ther-
mophilic microaerobic pretreated sample was 10.40% higher than
that of untreated sample. The maximum VS removal efﬁciency
was obtained from the sample that the oxygen loads was 10 ml/g
VS (VS of residual substrate) during the secondary thermophilic
microaerobic treatment. It was 29.43% and 17.23% higher than
those of untreated and once thermophilic microaerobic pretreated
samples, respectively. The higher VS removal efﬁciency means
more substrate was digested in anaerobic digestion, which would
be better for the reduction of fermentation residue.
4. Conclusions
Secondary thermophilic microaerobic treatment during the
batch anaerobic digestion of corn straw obviously improves the
methane yield and VS removal efﬁciency. The maximum methane
yield was obtained when the oxygen loads during STMT was 10 ml/
g VS (VS of residual substrate), which was respectively 28.45% and
10.61% higher than those of untreated and once thermophilic
microaerobic pretreated samples. The maximum VS removal efﬁ-
ciency was also obtained when the oxygen loads during STMT
was 10 ml/g VS (VS of residual substrate), which was respectively
29.43% and 17.23% higher than those of untreated and once ther-
mophilic microaerobic pretreated samples.
